Name: Ratha Yatra
Description / Significance: The chariot procession of Jagannath, Balabhadra, and Subhadra, in which the deities leave the temple sanctum to travel among the public — symbolically making devotion accessible to everyone, regardless of caste or status.

Name: Snana Yatra
Description / Significance: The ceremonial bathing of the deities on the full moon of Jyestha, using 108 pots of water, after which the deities are believed to fall ill and enter seclusion (Anasara).

Name: Chandan Yatra
Description / Significance: A 21-day sandalwood-anointing festival where representative images of the deities are taken out on boats in a temple tank, one of the longest continuous festivals in the Jagannath ritual calendar.

Name: Deepabali
Description / Significance: Odisha's version of Diwali, marked by the lighting of lamps and, distinctively, the ritual of "Kauriya Kathi" where ancestors' souls are guided by burning jute sticks.

Name: Durga Puja
Description / Significance: A 10-day festival particularly notable in Cuttack for its silver and gold tarakasi (filigree) work adorning the goddess's idols and pandal decorations, a craft unique to the city.

Name: Shivaratri
Description / Significance: One of the most widely observed Saivite festivals in Odisha, marked by night-long vigils (Jagaraatra) especially by women, celebrated prominently at the Lokanath, Lingaraj, Kapilas, and Nrusinghnath temples.

Name: Janmastami
Description / Significance: Krishna's birth anniversary, observed with day-long fasting broken only at midnight when the symbolic birth is enacted in temples and household shrines.

Name: Saraswati Puja
Description / Significance: A festival primarily observed by students, who worship the goddess of learning ahead of academic pursuits, followed by ritual immersion of clay idols.

Name: Ganesh Puja
Description / Significance: Observed mainly by students and increasingly by the broader public, honoring Ganesh as the remover of obstacles before undertaking new endeavors.

Name: Bali Jatra
Description / Significance: A seven-day fair commemorating ancient Kalinga sailors who traded with Bali and Southeast Asia; held on the banks of the Mahanadi, it combines handicrafts, cuisine, and maritime memory in one event.

Name: Raja Parba
Description / Significance: A three-day festival celebrating womanhood and the earth's fertility at the onset of monsoon; unmarried girls are dressed up and given rest from work, with customs like avoiding barefoot walking observed throughout.

Name: Pua Jiuntia
Description / Significance: Observed by mothers in western Odisha who invoke the deity Dutibahana for their sons' long life and prosperity.

Name: Bhai Jiuntia
Description / Significance: The sister's counterpart to Pua Jiuntia, where women fast and worship Goddess Durga for their brothers' well-being, observed on the eighth day of the bright lunar fortnight.

Name: Nuakhai
Description / Significance: Western Odisha's most important harvest festival, where new rice is ritually offered to the local deity before anyone eats it, followed by community greetings of "Nuakhai Juhar."

Name: Sitalsasthi
Description / Significance: A festival re-enacting the wedding of Shiva and Parvati through an elaborate street procession, with community members playing the roles of both families.

Name: Kumar Purnima
Description / Significance: A full-moon festival where young unmarried women observe rituals believed to bring a good future husband, associated with worship of the moon.

Name: Makar Sankranti / Makar Mela
Description / Significance: Marks the sun's transition into Capricorn, observed with ritual river bathing for spiritual cleansing and tribal fairs showcasing crafts, dance, and music.

Name: Dola Yatra
Description / Significance: Odisha's own spring festival for Krishna, occurring around the same time as Holi elsewhere in India but with distinct local ritual forms.

Name: Gaja Lakshmi Puja
Description / Significance: Worship of the goddess of wealth, observed by households and business communities seeking prosperity.

Name: Gamha Purnima
Description / Significance: Odisha's version of the Rakhi festival, tied to agricultural and cattle-worship customs specific to the region alongside the sibling-protection ritual.

Name: Pana Sankranti
Description / Significance: The Odia solar new year, reflecting the state's agrarian roots, marked by charitable acts and the preparation of "pana," a cooling seasonal drink.

Name: Kartik Purnima / Boita Bandana
Description / Significance: Commemorates ancestral Kalinga sailors by floating miniature paper and leaf boats in rivers and ponds, one of the most visually distinctive rituals unique to coastal Odisha.

Name: Ratha Saptami
Description / Significance: A sun-worship festival marking a directional shift of the sun god, observed primarily at sun temples.

Name: Prathamastami
Description / Significance: A festival specifically honoring the eldest child in a family, a custom less commonly found in other Indian regional calendars.

Name: Akshaya Tritiya
Description / Significance: An auspicious day that, in Odisha, doubles as the traditional start date for constructing the year's Rath Yatra chariots — linking a pan-Indian festival to a distinctly local ritual practice.

Name: Suna Besha
Description / Significance: A special evening when the deities appear in elaborate gold ornaments atop the chariots, drawing especially large crowds during the Rath Yatra period.

Name: Kandhen Budhi Yatra
Description / Significance: A tribal festival of the Kondh community, reflecting earth and ancestor worship traditions distinct from the Hindu temple calendar.

Name: Chhau Festival
Description / Significance: A dedicated festival showcasing the region's masked martial dance tradition, drawing performers and audiences from across the district.

Name: Toshali National Crafts Mela
Description / Significance: An annual crafts fair that brings artisans from across India (not just Odisha) together, serving as a major economic and cultural platform for craft preservation.

Name: Konark Dance Festival
Description / Significance:
An annual event where classical Indian dance forms are performed live against the backdrop of the illuminated Sun Temple, blending performance art with monument tourism.
